I moved to the high desert of New Mexico from the suburbs of New Jersey about 10 years ago. Suffering from chronic health problems, I was largely housebound by the pollution in NJ and unable to develop a home business because my hyper-religious hyper-conservative relatives felt such activity was unseemly. I was only able to tolerate the home there because it was built in the 1930s and my elderly relatives were so utterly change-averse they refused to improve the house in any way, leaving it largely free of the latently toxic materials common to most US houses as the building industry adopted its 'better living through chemistry' obsession. When the last of those relatives died, the home was slated to be sold, leaving me with with a small inheritance but nowhere to go as little clean housing exists anywhere on the east coast. Luckily, an online friend I had met through a space advocacy group I was long involved in knew of some rental cottages in New Mexico that were hand-built by a fellow who was a natural building advocate and follower of the legendary owner-builder guru Ken Kern. He also offered to teach me the basic workings of the college textbook trade which offered means for me to earn a modest living from home trading books online. And so I packed up my things in the old car I inherited, abandoning many of my prized books (I used to boast that I had a thousand books and one pair of shoes), and drove alone out to the west.

I now live alone in a small adobe cottage on a mesa south of Santa Fe. It's quiet but, of course, lonely. I've had to adapt to some things, like Internet by long-haul WiFi, chronic roof leaks and poor insulation from the rather rustic house construction, only shopping once a week, water that has to be brought in by truck every month, and dealing with the wildlife that tries to creep in occasionally. The book business seemed briefly promising, but in practice has never done much more than keep the roof over my head. It's proven far more stressful than it's worth. The Machiavellian machinations of the college textbook publishers are a constant hassle--particularly in the past year where they've been directly harassing me incessantly. It's pretty clear the textbook industry--if not the entire higher education industry--is heading for a major and imminent catastrophe thanks to runaway profiteering and mob-like business tactics. Because my hobbies have long revolved around alternative architecture and Post-Industrial futurism, I've long been involved in the P2P, Maker, Open Tech, and Open Manufacturing movements and have been looking to start a new home business deriving from this. I'd like to get into CNC based Tiny House and relief shelter development deriving from WikiHouse construction, but my efforts to save for a workshop have been stymied.
